question: Can finite-sample kernel-regression scaling exponents be derived from a polynomial covariance-spectrum tail and then transferred, without changing the exponent, to transformed representations, dependent samples, finite random-feature models, mixtures, and Transformers?

key_findings.claim: The substantive v1 claims that balancing a source-condition bias term against an effective-dimension variance term gives excess risk proportional to n^{-2s/(2s+1/beta)}.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 starts from E <= A lambda^{2s}+B sigma^2 n^{-1} lambda^{-1/beta}, chooses lambda proportional to n^{-1/(2s+1/beta)}, and reports alpha=2s/(2s+1/beta). This is an asymptotic kernel-ridge calculation, not a finite-n equality or a theorem about language-model loss.

key_findings.claim: The stated spectral assumption makes the core effective-dimension calculation divergent, so the main theorem is not valid as written.
key_findings.evidence: Assumption R sets lambda_i asymptotic to i^{-1/beta} with beta>1. Its exponent 1/beta is below one, so a covariance operator with this infinite sequence is not trace class and sum_i lambda_i/(lambda_i+lambda) diverges for every positive lambda. Appendix A.1 nevertheless treats the infinite tail integral as finite and concludes N_eff(lambda) asymptotic to lambda^{-1/beta}. A likely intended convention is lambda_i asymptotic to i^{-beta}, but that correction is reviewer inference and is not the pinned text.

key_findings.claim: The paper's verbal redundancy ordering is internally reversed relative to its own eigenvalue formula.
key_findings.evidence: It repeatedly says larger beta gives a steeper, more concentrated spectrum, yet under lambda_i proportional to i^{-1/beta}, increasing beta decreases the decay exponent and makes the tail flatter. The monotonic derivative of the reported alpha is algebraically consistent with its formula but not with the claimed spectral interpretation.

key_findings.claim: The finite-width theorem does not follow from the supplied perturbation argument.
key_findings.evidence: A fixed m-feature operator has rank at most m and therefore cannot share an infinite polynomial eigenvalue tail. Appendix A.10 applies an operator-norm error in the regime lambda_i(T_K) much larger than m^{-r}; that describes only finitely many leading modes, not 'all sufficiently large i.' Moreover, substituting lambda_star into the paper's own m^{-r} lambda^{-1/beta} term gives a different width requirement from m >= n^{r/(2s+1/beta)} as stated.

key_findings.claim: The Transformer results assume the decisive spectral and optimization properties instead of deriving them from a Transformer.
key_findings.evidence: T1 assumes a polynomial Transformer-NTK tail, bi-Lipschitz LayerNorm and residual maps on the data manifold, and a sum-of-heads/layers kernel representation; T2 assumes early-stopped SGD is ridge; T3 assumes adiabatic tail stability and bounded cumulative resolvent drift. Theorems 6-7 then reuse the kernel bias-variance calculation, and Appendix A.13-A.15 contains only this substitution and comparison argument.

key_findings.claim: The numerical section supports only controlled synthetic phenomena and does not test the claimed law on a trained deep model or natural dataset.
key_findings.evidence: The experiments use constructed bounded transforms, AR(1) dependence, a two-operator spectral mixture, random Fourier features, and Gaussian kernel-regression spectra. The representative fit beta=2 and s=0.5 is reported near alpha=0.67, and finite-width curves show visible intermediate humps. No real-data covariance tail, Transformer training curve, uncertainty interval, or out-of-range prediction is reported.

key_findings.claim: The quantity called redundancy is not directly observable in the settings for which the strongest claims are made.
key_findings.evidence: Even after repairing the tail convention, beta is an infinite-rank tail exponent of a chosen data-representation or effective-kernel operator, while s is smoothness of the unknown target in that same eigenbasis. Finite samples reveal only a noisy, cutoff-dependent spectrum, and the paper gives neither an estimator nor uncertainty propagation for beta, s, or beta_tr. Thus the proposed forecast requires latent quantities whose operational measurement is left open.

method.core_idea: Model sample scaling as the bias-variance tradeoff of kernel ridge regression, identify effective dimension with a covariance-tail power law, and transport the resulting exponent through operator comparisons and assumed effective kernels.
method.mechanism: Impose a polynomial eigenvalue tail and a source condition, upper-bound bias by lambda^{2s} and variance by n^{-1}N_eff(lambda), optimize lambda, then invoke bounded invertibility, positive-operator mixtures, mixing-based effective sample size, random-feature perturbation, Transformer NTKs, and a time-averaged drifting kernel. Synthetic experiments instantiate each proposed invariance separately.
assumptions: The pinned text assumes lambda_i is comparable to i^{-1/beta} for beta>1; as written this is not a trace-class covariance spectrum and invalidates the finite effective dimension.
The target satisfies an infinite-dimensional source condition f_star=T_K^s g with unknown s>0 and bounded g coefficients.
Kernel ridge uses an i.i.d. noise model for the core result; the dependent extension assumes stationary beta-mixing, finite 2+gamma moments, and summable transformed mixing coefficients.
Representation changes are boundedly invertible linear maps with uniform frame bounds; destructive compression and noninvertible feature learning are outside this result.
The mixture theorem treats positive operator sums and presumes the individual tail asymptotics are meaningful under the same ambient operator setup.
The random-feature extension assumes operator and trace-resolvent approximation bounds with an unspecified exponent r and ignores the finite-rank tail obstruction in its proof.

Transformer transfer assumes rather than derives the effective NTK tail, bi-Lipschitz residual/LayerNorm behavior, head/layer kernel decomposition, ridge-equivalent SGD, and stable source condition under kernel drift.

All displayed rates are asymptotic order statements; no finite-sample constants, confidence intervals, minimax lower bound for the proposed redundancy index, or regime-identification procedure is supplied.

techniques.role: Balances source-condition ridge bias against a trace-resolvent variance term to obtain an exponent.
Attempts to convert eigenvalue regular variation into an effective-dimension power law; the pinned derivation fails under its stated exponent convention.
Uses min-max comparisons under boundedly invertible feature transforms to preserve eigenvalue order up to constants.
Uses positivity and eigenvalue comparisons to attribute a mixture's asymptotic behavior to its slowest-decaying component.
Replaces n with an assumed effective sample size in the variance term for beta-mixing sequences.
Bounds a time-averaged effective kernel between assumed spectral envelopes rather than solving nonlinear feature-learning dynamics.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic kernel regression after an identity representation or one of three boundedly invertible random rotation-plus-diagonal transforms
evaluations.metric: Log-log excess-risk curve versus sample size and fitted slope
evaluations.result: Curves are reported to nearly overlap and have similar slopes
evaluations.baseline: Identity representation under the same synthetic data and kernel

evaluations.setting: Synthetic AR(1) samples with autocorrelation rho in {0.2, 0.5, 0.8}
evaluations.metric: Excess risk versus raw n and versus n_eff=n(1-rho)/(1+rho)
evaluations.result: Raw curves shift vertically and visually collapse after the effective-sample-size rescaling
evaluations.baseline: The same learning curves plotted against raw sample size

evaluations.setting: Convex mixture of two synthetic covariance operators with beta_1=1.3, beta_2=2.5 and weights 0.6, 0.4
evaluations.result: The plotted curve is reported to align with the component labeled as the heavier tail
evaluations.baseline: Predictions based on the lighter component or an average tail index

evaluations.setting: Random Fourier feature approximations with widths m in {50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000}
evaluations.metric: Excess-risk curve under the theoretical regularization schedule
evaluations.result: Small and intermediate widths show humps; widths at least 1000 visually approach the kernel curve

evaluations.setting: Controlled Gaussian kernel-regression examples varying target smoothness s and the paper's beta parameter
evaluations.result: For beta=2 and s=0.5 the fitted slope is described as close to the predicted alpha=0.67; other panels show qualitative slope ordering
evaluations.baseline: The exponent formula alpha=2s/(2s+1/beta), with no numerical uncertainty reported

limitations: Source-status limitation: this reading deliberately audits the substantive arXiv v1 pinned by source override. The current arXiv revision is a withdrawn 1 KB v2; retaining v1 for forensic review must not be read as current author endorsement or atlas endorsement.
Author-stated: polynomial tails and the source condition need not hold for non-polynomial or real data spectra.
Author-stated: summable beta-mixing may miss long-range dependence, and sublinear effective sample growth could change the observed regime.
Author-stated: finite-width and Transformer sections rely on approximation assumptions that can fail under abrupt kernel shifts or insufficient width.
Author-stated: beta_tr is not derived from attention, positional encodings, or other architectural primitives, and real-data validation is absent.
Reviewer-identified: the main spectral convention makes the covariance non-trace-class, the effective dimension infinite, and the redundancy ordering opposite to the prose.
Reviewer-identified: the bias proof on page 13 invokes s-1>=0 although the stated assumption is only s>0, and the strict-convexity claim also fails as written for part of that range.
Reviewer-identified: the random-feature tail-preservation and width-growth arguments are mathematically incompatible with a fixed finite-rank feature operator.
Reviewer-identified: no Transformer, natural dataset, real covariance spectrum, or forward extrapolation of a scaling curve is evaluated.
failure_modes: Using the pinned beta convention yields infinite effective dimension, so every downstream exponent and universality statement built on it loses its premise.
Repairing the apparent exponent typo does not automatically repair the source-condition range, finite-width calculation, or Transformer assumptions.
Finite-sample tail fits are dominated by rank cutoff, noise, regularization, and representation choice, making beta and therefore the predicted alpha unstable.
A noninvertible representation change, learned bottleneck, or feature collapse can change both target smoothness and spectrum, outside the representation-invariance theorem.
Mixture weights that vanish with sample size, nonstationary domains, or noncommuting task-specific operators can produce crossovers rather than one stable tail exponent.
Long-range sequence dependence can change the sample-size clock non-polynomially, so plotting against raw tokens need not retain the claimed exponent.
Feature learning with phase transitions violates adiabatic resolvent drift; an averaged kernel can conceal distinct training regimes.
Optimizing or deduplicating data to steepen a finite empirical spectrum may discard rare predictive modes and change s, so the monotone prescription need not improve risk.
reusable_insights: A credible spectral scaling theory must state a trace-class eigenvalue convention and verify that its effective dimension is finite before optimizing a bias-variance bound.
Separate an observable finite-rank spectral fit from an infinite-tail parameter, and propagate cutoff and estimator uncertainty into any predicted learning exponent.
Treat data spectrum and target alignment jointly: changing representations can improve apparent compressibility while making the target rougher in the new eigenbasis.
Use designed transformation, dependence, mixture, and width interventions as stress tests, but do not call them architectural universality without natural-data and trained-model evidence.
For finite-width approximations, compare the learned spectral band only up to rank m and include the approximation plateau or crossover explicitly.
Source revision status is part of scientific provenance: a withdrawn current revision should remain visibly distinct from a deliberately pinned historical text.
open_questions: After replacing lambda_i proportional to i^{-1/beta} with a valid trace-class convention, which stated theorems survive with correct constants and source-condition ranges?
What is the correct joint condition on width m, sample size n, and regularization lambda for preserving risk rates without pretending a finite-rank operator has an infinite tail?
Can beta and s be estimated with honest uncertainty from finite real representations, and do their estimates predict held-out scaling slopes beyond the fitted range?
Does deduplication change only the covariance tail, or also remove rare target-relevant directions enough to offset any effective-dimension benefit?
Which Transformer components provably determine the effective-kernel spectrum without assuming the desired tail in T1?
How do abrupt feature-learning transitions or changing spectral exponents alter the time-dependent learning curve?
Can mixture crossovers and long-range sequence dependence explain broken rather than single power laws in real training runs?
What specific technical issue led to withdrawal, and is there a corrected author-supported theorem in a separate future record?

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Kaplan et al. fit language-model loss across model size, data, and compute over many orders of magnitude and derive compute-allocation rules. The audited v1 instead proposes a kernel-ridge sample exponent from a covariance tail and does not test language models.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Hoffmann et al. train more than 400 language models and revise the model-token compute optimum using observed loss and downstream tasks. The audited v1 supplies no compute allocation across parameters and tokens and no large-model experiment; it studies an asymptotic sample-rate surrogate.

competitive_landscape.title: Explaining Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Bahri et al. distinguish variance- and resolution-limited regimes for data and model size, relate kernel spectra to a manifold-resolution picture, and test standard architectures and datasets. The audited v1 collapses the explanation to one claimed redundancy index and offers only synthetic kernel experiments.

competitive_landscape.title: A Dynamical Model of Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Bordelon et al. solve gradient-descent dynamics in a random-feature model and separate training-time, width, finite-data reuse, and compute-optimal effects. The audited v1 starts from a ridge bias-variance bound and assumes SGD-to-ridge and stable kernel drift rather than deriving training dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: A Solvable Model of Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Maloney et al. jointly specify a generative data model and nonlinear random-feature model, derive parameter-data bottlenecks, and expose plateaus from finite spectral extent. The audited v1 asserts a general covariance-tail law and does not model finite spectral ranges or joint data-parameter saturation correctly.

competitive_landscape.title: How Feature Learning Can Improve Neural Scaling Laws
competitive_landscape.difference: Bordelon et al. solve a beyond-kernel feature-learning model, distinguish hard from RKHS-easy tasks, and validate with nonlinear MLPs and CNNs. The audited v1 assumes adiabatic kernel-tail envelopes and concludes monotonic improvement if the tail steepens, without deriving when real feature learning does so.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically
competitive_landscape.difference: Hestness et al. measure generalization and model-size scaling across translation, language, vision, and speech and observe architecture changes mainly shifting levels. The audited v1 claims a universal spectral mechanism but supplies no comparable cross-domain measurement.

competitive_landscape.title: Theory of Scaling Laws for In-Context Regression: Depth, Width, Context and Time
competitive_landscape.difference: Bordelon, Letey, and Pehlevan derive separate asymptotic bottlenecks for time, width, depth, and context in a deep linear-attention ICL model and show task-distribution dependence. The audited v1 gives one sample exponent and transfers it to Transformers only through assumed effective-kernel properties.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The pinned v1 claims the first rigorous mathematical explanation of empirical scaling laws as finite-sample redundancy laws, with a closed-form exponent universal across representations, mixtures, finite width, dependence, and Transformer regimes.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The claimed contribution is assembled in Theorems 1-7 and synthetic Figures 2-7, but the current arXiv revision is withdrawn and the core v1 derivation is invalid under its written spectrum convention.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The potentially useful intuition is to connect target alignment and an effective spectral dimension and to stress-test invariances. It is not a valid new law in the pinned form: prior work already derives spectral/kernel scaling regimes and dynamic finite-resource laws, while v1's non-trace-class tail, reversed interpretation, and finite-rank contradiction defeat its central theorem. This audit records historical content and errors, not current endorsement.

reviewer_notes: Atomic review covered all 15 extracted pages, including every proof appendix. The exact override intentionally pins substantive arXiv v1. The arXiv record checked 2026-08-23 states that the newer/current v2 is withdrawn; nothing in this reading should imply current author support or atlas endorsement. Primary competitor records and current versions were inspected directly. Formula audits independently checked trace-class summability, the effective-dimension series, monotonicity of i^{-1/beta}, source-condition range language, and the finite-rank random-feature argument.
